cards.front: Which enzyme converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II, and where is it mainly found?
cards.back: Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE), a dipeptidyl carboxypeptidase on the luminal surface of endothelial cells, especially in the lungs. Ang I is only about one hundredth as potent as Ang II, so this conversion is the key activation step.

cards.front: What is captopril, and what does it block?
cards.back: A sulfhydryl-containing dipeptide analogue of proline and the first orally active ACE inhibitor. It blocks conversion of Ang I to Ang II and slows bradykinin breakdown. It does not block AT1 or AT2 receptors.

cards.front: Why do ACE inhibitors cause cough, and what is done about it?
cards.back: ACE normally degrades bradykinin and substance P, so both accumulate in the lungs of susceptible patients. The dry cough is not dose related and usually appears within weeks of starting. It often needs the drug stopped, though it settles within days of withdrawal. ARBs rarely cause it and serve as a substitute.

cards.front: How do ARBs differ from ACE inhibitors pharmacologically?
cards.back: ARBs block the AT1 receptor directly and do not inhibit ACE, so bradykinin and substance P are not raised and cough is rare. They also block Ang II formed by non-ACE routes, giving more complete AT1 blockade. Ang II rises by feedback, so unblocked AT2 receptors are more stimulated. ARBs raise Ang (1-7) much less than ACE inhibitors do.

cards.front: Why are ACE inhibitors and ARBs contraindicated in pregnancy?
cards.back: They are fetotoxic. Exposure in the second and third trimesters causes fetal growth retardation, organ hypoplasia and fetal death. First-trimester exposure has been linked to malformations. The drug must be stopped as soon as pregnancy is detected.

cards.front: Which patients are at risk of acute renal failure when an ACE inhibitor is started?
cards.back: Patients with bilateral renal artery stenosis, or stenosis of the artery to a solitary kidney, because glomerular filtration in these kidneys depends on angiotensin II constricting the efferent arteriole. The risk rises with NSAIDs, diuretics and volume depletion.

cards.front: What is the captopril test, and what are its limits?
cards.back: Acute captopril blockade of Ang II formation causes a reflex rise in plasma renin activity. The rise is much larger in renovascular hypertension than in essential hypertension. It was designed to avoid renal angiography, but it is only an adjunct test.

cards.front: What is the mortality benefit of ACE inhibitors in heart failure, and how are they dosed?
cards.back: They reduce mortality by roughly 20% in symptomatic heart failure and slow remodelling, and they have long been first line for systolic dysfunction at all NYHA grades unless contraindicated. Start low, especially with diuretics, then titrate toward target doses; in the ATLAS trial, higher-dose lisinopril reduced death and heart-failure hospitalisation more than low dose. Sacubitril-valsartan was superior to enalapril (PARADIGM-HF) and is now recommended to replace an ACE inhibitor or ARB in NYHA II to III HFrEF.

cards.front: What is the rationale and the main risk of combining an ACE inhibitor with an ARB?
cards.back: Rationale: angiotensin II is also formed by non-ACE routes that an ARB can block, and ARBs cause a compensatory angiotensin II rise that an ACE inhibitor can limit. In practice the combination increases hyperkalaemia, hypotension and renal impairment, and trial evidence (ONTARGET) does not support combining an ACE inhibitor with an ARB in hypertension, heart failure or nephropathy. Aliskiren should likewise not be added to an ACE inhibitor or ARB in diabetics (ALTITUDE).

cards.front: Where and how does the direct renin inhibitor aliskiren act?
cards.back: It binds selectively to the catalytic site of renin and blocks access of angiotensinogen, so Ang I is not formed. This is the rate-limiting step. Renin concentration rises by feedback, but plasma renin activity falls, and Ang I and Ang II fall in a dose-dependent way.

cards.front: What are the pharmacokinetic and safety features of aliskiren?
cards.back: Oral bioavailability is very low because P-glycoprotein pumps the absorbed drug back out. It is mainly eliminated in faeces, has a half-life over 24 hours, and its BP effect persists for days. Adverse effects are mild (dyspepsia, abdominal pain, loose stools, headache, dizziness). It is contraindicated in pregnancy. Adding it to an ACE inhibitor or ARB in type 2 diabetes is not advised.

cards.front: Classify: sites of renin-angiotensin system inhibition
cards.text: {{Beta-blockers}} reduce renin release; {{aliskiren}} blocks renin itself; {{ACE inhibitors}} block Ang I to Ang II conversion; {{ARBs}} block the AT1 receptor; {{spironolactone}} blocks the mineralocorticoid receptor.

cards.front: How is nitric oxide formed, and what makes it unusual as a signal molecule?
cards.back: NO is made from L-arginine by nitric oxide synthase, using O2 and NADPH, with FMN, FAD, haem and tetrahydrobiopterin as cofactors. It is the smallest endogenous signal molecule and a gas at body temperature. It has no stored pool, diffuses across membranes rather than being exocytosed, and lasts only seconds.

cards.front: How do the constitutive NOS isoforms differ from iNOS?
cards.back: eNOS and nNOS are constitutive and Ca2+-calmodulin dependent, producing small amounts on demand. iNOS is induced by endotoxin, cytokines and TNF-alpha in macrophages and other cells. It is Ca2+ independent and produces large amounts over hours to days.

cards.front: What is the signalling pathway by which NO relaxes vascular smooth muscle?
cards.back: NO diffuses into smooth muscle and activates soluble guanylyl cyclase, raising cGMP. cGMP activates protein kinase G, which lowers cytosolic Ca2+ (less Ca2+ entry) and reduces myosin light-chain phosphorylation, both by decreasing myosin light-chain kinase activity and by increasing myosin light-chain phosphatase activity. Actin-myosin interaction falls and the muscle relaxes.

cards.front: Which enzyme releases NO from glyceryl trinitrate, and why does tolerance develop?
cards.back: Mitochondrial aldehyde dehydrogenase, which is abundant in veins and explains the venodilator preference of GTN. Continuous exposure generates reactive oxygen species that inhibit this enzyme. Tolerance develops within hours and wears off quickly off the drug.

cards.front: What is the mechanism and key toxicity of sodium nitroprusside?
cards.back: It releases NO (in red cells and other tissues, partly non-enzymatically by reaction with glutathione) and also directly activates guanylyl cyclase, dilating arterioles and veins equally. Its action is very rapid, titratable and brief, and nitrate-like tolerance does not develop. The cyanide released is converted by mitochondrial rhodanese, using a sulfur donor, to thiocyanate, which the kidney excretes slowly. High-rate infusion can cause cyanide toxicity (metabolic acidosis, arrhythmias, death); sodium thiosulfate or hydroxocobalamin is used for prevention or treatment. Prolonged infusion, especially in renal failure, lets thiocyanate accumulate (weakness, disorientation, psychosis, convulsions).

cards.front: What are the actions of the natriuretic peptides, and how do they relate to the renin-angiotensin system?
cards.back: ANP (mainly atrial) and BNP (mainly ventricular) cause vasodilatation, natriuresis and diuresis. They lower renin release, Ang II and aldosterone, counter-regulating the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system. CNP acts mainly as a vasodilator with little natriuretic effect.

cards.front: What is the source and basic structure of cardiac glycosides?
cards.back: Digoxin is obtained from Digitalis lanata and is the only glycoside still in clinical use. A cardiac glycoside is a steroid-based aglycone (genin) with an unsaturated lactone ring, carrying one or more sugar moieties.

cards.front: How does digoxin increase myocardial contractility?
cards.back: It inhibits the membrane Na+/K+ ATPase from the outer surface of the cell. Intracellular Na+ rises, so Na+/Ca2+ exchange extrudes less Ca2+ and the sarcoplasmic reticulum becomes overloaded. Subsequent calcium transients are larger. The inotropic effect takes hours to develop because binding is slow.

cards.front: How does digoxin slow the heart, and why is bradycardia more marked in heart failure?
cards.back: Digoxin increases vagal tone and directly depresses the SA and AV nodes, slowing AV conduction and prolonging AV nodal refractoriness. In heart failure, better output withdraws sympathetic overactivity and restores vagal tone, so the bradycardia is greater.

cards.front: What are the early features of digoxin toxicity?
cards.back: Anorexia, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain and diarrhoea, along with confusion, headache and visual disturbances. These extracardiac features usually precede cardiac toxicity, in about two-thirds of toxic patients. Further doses must be stopped at the first sign of toxicity.

cards.front: Which factors predispose to digoxin toxicity?
cards.back: Hypokalaemia (a key precipitant), high calcium, advanced age, renal insufficiency, severe hepatic disease and thyrotoxicosis. Interacting drugs such as quinidine, verapamil and amiodarone raise plasma digoxin levels.

cards.front: How is digoxin-induced ventricular arrhythmia treated, and which drugs should be avoided?
cards.back: IV lidocaine, repeated as needed; it suppresses excess automaticity without worsening AV block. Quinidine, procainamide and propafenone should be avoided. Potassium is given for tachyarrhythmia only when potassium is low, and never with a high degree of AV block.

cards.front: What is digoxin-specific Fab antibody used for?
cards.back: Fab fragments bind digoxin and related glycosides and rapidly reverse severe, life-threatening toxicity. They are non-immunogenic because they lack the Fc fragment, and are given by IV infusion.

cards.front: Where does digoxin fit in atrial fibrillation rate control and in PSVT?
cards.back: In AF or flutter, digoxin slows the ventricular rate but does not restore sinus rhythm, and it acts slowly. Beta-blockers or non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers are preferred for rapid control, while digoxin suits AF with heart failure. In PSVT, adenosine, verapamil or esmolol act faster and are preferred to digoxin.

cards.front: What is the evidence for digoxin in heart failure?
cards.back: It relieves symptoms and reduces decompensation and heart-failure hospitalisation, particularly with low ejection fraction. The DIG trial showed no reduction in overall mortality. Digoxin does not reverse or slow the pathological remodelling of heart failure, and it can be withdrawn in some stable patients in sinus rhythm.

cards.front: Ivabradine: mechanism, indication and place in heart failure therapy?
cards.back: It selectively blocks the hyperpolarisation-activated (HCN) pacemaker channels that carry the funny current in the sinoatrial node, lowering heart rate without a direct inotropic or vasodilator effect. It is indicated in stable NYHA II to IV heart failure with sinus rhythm, heart rate above 70/min and LVEF 35% or less, when a beta-blocker is contraindicated or an adequate beta-blocker dose does not bring the rate down enough. Added to standard therapy, it reduced heart-failure hospitalisation and heart-failure deaths, but not total or cardiovascular mortality (SHIFT), and it lacks the cardioprotective effects of beta-blockers.

cards.front: Which drug classes reduce mortality in systolic heart failure?
cards.back: ACE inhibitors or ARBs, or sacubitril-valsartan (which is now recommended in place of them); evidence-based beta-blockers (metoprolol succinate, bisoprolol, carvedilol, nebivolol); mineralocorticoid antagonists (spironolactone, eplerenone); and SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin), the most recent addition, which reduce mortality and HF hospitalisation with or without diabetes. Diuretics relieve congestion but do not improve survival; digoxin reduces hospitalisation without reducing overall mortality.

cards.front: Where do SGLT2 inhibitors fit in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction?
cards.back: Dapagliflozin and empagliflozin, developed as antidiabetic drugs, reduce mortality and heart-failure hospitalisation in HFrEF whether or not the patient has diabetes, and this appears to be a class effect. Dapagliflozin was the first approved for heart failure (USA, 2020); empagliflozin is approved for both HFrEF and HFpEF, and SGLT2 inhibitors are now considered first-line for HFpEF. They are added to the other prognostic drugs (ACE inhibitor, ARB or sacubitril-valsartan, beta-blocker and MRA). The mechanism is not settled: SGLT2 is absent from the heart, so natriuresis and glycosuria with preload reduction ("a better diuretic") is likely, with possible off-target effects such as sodium-hydrogen exchanger inhibition and less myocardial glucose use. They also slow chronic kidney disease. Adverse effects include genital and urinary tract infections and ketoacidosis.

cards.text: Digoxin is excreted {{unchanged}} in urine mainly by {{glomerular filtration}}; its half-life is about {{1.5 to 2 days}}, and it is a {{cumulative}} drug.

cards.front: Classify: factors that increase digoxin toxicity
cards.text: {{Hypokalaemia}} and high {{calcium}} increase toxicity; {{quinidine}}, {{verapamil}} and {{amiodarone}} raise plasma digoxin levels; {{thyrotoxicosis}} increases susceptibility to arrhythmia.

cards.front: Classify: management of digoxin toxicity
cards.text: For ventricular arrhythmias give IV {{lidocaine}}; {{quinidine}} and {{procainamide}} are avoided; AV block with bradycardia is treated with a {{temporary pacemaker}}; DC {{cardioversion}} is avoided.

cards.front: Classify: drugs in heart failure by purpose
cards.text: Positive inotropes include {{digoxin}}, {{dobutamine}} and {{levosimendan}}; loop {{diuretics}} relieve congestion; {{spironolactone}} and {{eplerenone}} are aldosterone antagonists that improve survival.

cards.front: Classify: vasodilators and the heart-rate-lowering drug
cards.text: {{Nitrates}} mainly dilate veins, {{hydralazine}} mainly dilates arterioles, and {{sodium nitroprusside}} dilates both; {{ivabradine}} acts on the {{sinoatrial node}} to slow the heart rate.

cards.front: Short note: Newer drugs in heart failure

points: Dapagliflozin, empagliflozin: reduce mortality and HF hospitalisation in HFrEF with or without diabetes; empagliflozin also approved in HFpEF
Probably act through natriuresis and preload reduction; genital and urinary infections, ketoacidosis
Neprilysin inhibition raises natriuretic peptides; valsartan blocks AT1
Superior to enalapril; recommended in place of an ACE inhibitor or ARB; never with an ACE inhibitor
Soluble guanylyl cyclase stimulator that also sensitises the enzyme to NO (like riociguat, but longer acting)
In advanced HFrEF after recent hospitalisation, added to standard therapy, it reduced CV death or first HF hospitalisation by about 10%
Symptomatic hypotension slightly more common
Non-steroidal mineralocorticoid antagonist (approved 2021); more selective, possibly less hyperkalaemia
HCN (funny current) blocker for sinus rhythm with heart rate above 70/min despite beta-blockade; fewer HF hospitalisations and HF deaths
In iron deficiency, improves symptoms, NYHA class and exercise capacity; after acute HF it reduced HF hospitalisation but not CV death
